title: Blue, Clubbed, Loud P2, No Murmur / The Defect Has Gone Quiet

blocks.text: Blue, Clubbed, Loud P2, No Murmur / The Defect Has Gone Quiet

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-09 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension (2022); ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular disease and pregnancy (2025) · Related AMaC: AMaC atrial septal defect station; this one tests a shunt that has reversed
The patient is a woman of 31 who works in a library. She has been breathless on gentle exertion for years and is always tired. Please examine her cardiovascular system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A blue, clubbed patient with a loud palpable P2 and no shunt murmur has Eisenmenger syndrome. The murmur of her original defect has disappeared because the shunt has reversed.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates look for the murmur, hear none and call the heart normal, or advise closing the defect. Pass: cyanosis, clubbing, loud P2 and no shunt murmur, so Eisenmenger. Fail: normal heart, or closure.

rows: She is blue at rest: look at the lips, hands and face before you touch her.
"May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; look at lips, hands, face, eyes; pulse; JVP.
Feel for a heave and a palpable second sound, then listen for what is missing.
"I'm going to feel your chest and listen over the heart, then lean you forward."
Heave; thrill; P2; four areas; Graham Steell murmur; lung bases; ankles; cover her; clean hands.
Say the diagnosis, why the murmur is missing, and what pregnancy means for her.
"She has Eisenmenger syndrome, probably from an unrepaired ventricular septal defect. Pregnancy is not recommended: the risk to her life is very high."
Present in order; diagnosis; complications; pregnancy and contraception; specialist care; thank her.
Starts without consent; asks her to lie flat despite breathlessness; leaves her exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits her at 45 degrees, covers her afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone, pauses if she is breathless, and keeps exposure to the minimum.
Disorganised; omits the lips, hands, heave or P2.
Looks at lips, hands and face, then pulse, JVP, heave, palpable P2, four auscultation areas, lung bases and ankles.
Also leans her forward in held expiration and looks for a plethoric face.
Reports a pansystolic murmur or a quiet second sound.
Finds central cyanosis, clubbing, a right ventricular heave, a loud palpable P2, a soft early diastolic murmur and no pansystolic murmur.
Also finds a plethoric face and a prominent JVP a wave, and states no thrill.
Calls it a normal heart, or tetralogy of Fallot.
Eisenmenger syndrome from an unrepaired ventricular septal defect.
Also explains the lost murmur: pressures have equalised and the shunt has reversed.
Names haemoptysis, thickened blood, iron deficiency, stroke and abscess, arrhythmia and endocarditis.
Also names gout, kidney stones and paradoxical embolism.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): says pregnancy is safe, or advises routine venesection or closure of the defect.
Says pregnancy is not recommended because the risk is very high, avoids oestrogen contraception, and refers to a specialist congenital and pulmonary hypertension centre.

Also says to avoid dehydration and altitude, that a levonorgestrel intrauterine or progestogen-only method is arranged with the specialist team, that termination is discussed early if she becomes pregnant, and that bosentan is recommended if she is symptomatic.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: thin, mildly breathless on speaking; respiratory rate 18; pulse 84 regular; blood pressure 108/70; SpO2 82% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Lips: blue. Hands: warm, clubbed. Face: plethoric. JVP raised with a prominent a wave. Apex beat not displaced; right ventricular heave; palpable loud second sound. No thrill. First sound normal; second sound loud and single; no pansystolic murmur; soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Lungs clear. Mild ankle swelling.

Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis and likely cause? (D) Told: a hole in the heart left untreated in childhood. 3. Why is there no murmur from the hole? (D) 4. Complications? (E) 5. What would you advise about pregnancy? (E)

Curveballs: She asks whether the hole can be closed now: not with a high pulmonary resistance; the specialist decides. Her haemoglobin is high: that alone is not an indication for venesection. Look for iron deficiency, dehydration and symptoms of hyperviscosity, and leave any phlebotomy to the specialist team. Flying? Specialist advice; avoid dehydration.
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and asks about pain (G)
Looks at lips, hands and face before touching her (A)
Feels for a right ventricular heave and a palpable P2 (A)
Finds central cyanosis, clubbing and a loud P2 (B)
States no pansystolic murmur and no thrill (B)
Names Eisenmenger syndrome and explains the missing murmur (D)
Lists haemoptysis, thickened blood, iron deficiency, stroke and abscess (E)
Says pregnancy is not recommended and avoids oestrogen contraception (E)
Refers to a specialist congenital and pulmonary hypertension centre (E)
Covers her, cleans hands and thanks her (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Lie flat. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens at the apex only.) [R2 Fail] The heart sounds are normal. [R3 Fail] It's tetralogy of Fallot. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Complications and advice?
CANDIDATE: Heart failure. [R5 Fail] Pregnancy is fine, and we should close the defect. [R6 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): pregnancy is not recommended in Eisenmenger syndrome and closure is unsafe with a high pulmonary resistance. No consent, no cyanosis or P2 found, and the diagnosis missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Lips, hands, face; pulse, JVP, heave, P2, four areas, bases, ankles.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: She is centrally cyanosed and clubbed, with a right ventricular heave, a loud palpable P2, a soft early diastolic murmur and no pansystolic murmur. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Eisenmenger syndrome from an unrepaired ventricular septal defect. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Complications?
CANDIDATE: Haemoptysis, thickened blood, iron deficiency, stroke and abscess, arrhythmia and endocarditis. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Pregnancy?
CANDIDATE: Not recommended; the risk is very high. Avoid oestrogen contraception, and refer to a specialist congenital and pulmonary hypertension centre. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not explain the missing murmur, the other complications or altitude and dehydration.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) May I examine your heart? Would you like a chaperone? I'll pause if you are breathless and keep you covered. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Lips, hands, plethoric face; JVP, heave, P2; leans her forward in held expiration; ankles.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Cyanosis, clubbing, plethoric face, prominent JVP a wave, heave, loud palpable P2, soft early diastolic murmur; no pansystolic murmur and no thrill. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands, thanks her.) [R1 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Eisenmenger syndrome. The defect's murmur has gone because pressures have equalised and the shunt has reversed. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Complications?
CANDIDATE: Haemoptysis, thickened blood, iron deficiency, stroke, abscess, gout, kidney stones, paradoxical embolism and endocarditis. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Pregnancy?

CANDIDATE: Not recommended, and early specialist counselling including termination if she became pregnant; no oestrogen, a levonorgestrel intrauterine or progestogen-only method with the specialist team. Specialist centre; avoid dehydration and altitude; bosentan if she is symptomatic. [R6 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone and pauses, the plethoric face, the reason for the missing murmur, the wider complications, and lifestyle and drug advice.
R3: Missing the cyanosis and clubbing. They are the signs that show the shunt has reversed, and without them the patient looks like a normal heart.
R4: Hunting for a murmur and calling the heart normal. The absence of the defect's murmur, with a loud P2, is the diagnosis.
R6: Advising closure of the defect. With a high pulmonary resistance it is unsafe; the examiner sees a red flag that the physiology has not been understood.
R6: Saying pregnancy is possible. It is not recommended in Eisenmenger syndrome because maternal mortality is very high.
"Let me look at her lips and hands again before I go on."
"There is no pansystolic murmur, but P2 is loud, so I'd reconsider Eisenmenger."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"

Eisenmenger syndrome: central cyanosis, clubbing, a right ventricular lift, an accentuated palpable second sound, a soft early diastolic (Graham Steell) murmur, and loss of the original defect's murmur.

Pregnancy carries a very high maternal risk in Eisenmenger syndrome and is not recommended (ESC/ERS 2022, Class III), and if she becomes pregnant, termination is discussed early (ESC 2025). Avoid oestrogen-containing contraception; levonorgestrel-based long-acting methods (implant or intrauterine device) are recommended, arranged with the specialist team (ESC/ERS 2022). Routine phlebotomy is not recommended (ESC/ERS 2022, Class III); for hyperviscosity symptoms with a haematocrit above 65%, hydrate and correct iron deficiency first. A high haemoglobin alone is not an indication. Routine anticoagulation is not given; it may be considered only for pulmonary artery thrombosis without significant haemoptysis (Class IIb).

Specialist adult congenital and pulmonary hypertension centre follow-up. Bosentan is recommended in symptomatic Eisenmenger syndrome to improve exercise capacity (ESC/ERS 2022, Class I); other pulmonary hypertension drugs are added by the specialist team.
THINK: Blue, clubbed, loud P2, no murmur: reversed shunt.
SAY: "Eisenmenger syndrome from an unrepaired defect."
DO: Look at lips and hands; feel the heave and P2.
NUMBERS: Haematocrit over 65% with hyperviscosity symptoms: hydrate and treat iron deficiency first; no routine phlebotomy (ESC/ERS 2022).
TRAP: Calling it normal, or closing the defect.
FINISH: Pregnancy not recommended; specialist centre; no oestrogen.

ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension (2022). Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac237 Supports: Eisenmenger syndrome (Recommendation Table 19): bosentan for symptomatic patients, pregnancy not recommended, routine phlebotomy not recommended, iron deficiency corrected, levonorgestrel-based contraception, anticoagulation only for pulmonary artery thrombosis.

ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular disease and pregnancy (2025). Eur Heart J 2025;46(43):4462-4568 (published online 29 August 2025). https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/43/4462/8234510 Supports: very high maternal risk in Eisenmenger syndrome and pulmonary arterial hypertension; discussion of termination; caution with combined oral contraception in cyanosis; levonorgestrel intrauterine device with caution and monitoring in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
